claims.text: The as-manufactured high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
The initial alloy has high toughness.
The initial alloy undergoes uniform ductile deformation.
Prolonged mechanical loading at elevated temperature induces microstructural evolution in the alloy.
The imposed service exposure causes elemental segregation at grain boundaries.
The imposed service exposure may cause nanoscale precipitates to form at grain boundaries.
Elevated temperature enables atomic diffusion that drives grain-boundary segregation or precipitation.
Grain-boundary segregation or precipitation reduces intergranular cohesion.
Reduced intergranular cohesion creates preferential sites for crack initiation and propagation under mechanical stress.
The grain-boundary changes promote a transition from ductile to brittle fracture.
Exposed samples will exhibit lower fracture toughness than the initial baseline.
Exposed samples will show more brittle fracture behavior than the initial baseline.
The hypothesis applies when loading temperature and duration are sufficient to promote atomic diffusion.
The proposed mechanism may not operate at low temperatures or over short service periods because diffusion is minimal.
Samples from the same batch can be divided into an elevated-temperature mechanically loaded set and a room-temperature or minimally loaded reference set.

The hypothesis is deemed falsified if exposed samples show neither significant grain-boundary segregation or nanoscale precipitation nor a statistically detectable toughness change relative to controls.
